title: 🐾 Eryndor Living Culture Atlas X — Animal Peoples, Diasporas & Mixed Communities
rawNotionMarkup: Eryndor Living Culture Atlas X — the eight sapient animal-featured peoples. Creator-established rule: each people has multiple subcultures, and regional conditions, class, religion, guilds, kin and individual biography matter. None of these peoples are ordinary animals; ordinary wolves, foxes, lions, tigers, elephants, bears, cattle and pigs also exist independently. Animal features can affect senses, clothing and mobility, but must not dictate morality, intelligence, profession, faith or family form. All reproductive facts, birth rates, populations and lifespans remain as established or unknown. These specific subculture labels and customs are new/revisable. ## All established peoples in western Avarra and the Urakai southeastern badlands — creator reminder (21 November 2026) Do not omit the eccentric/small/large folk: The creator specifically requires the expanded Avarran west and the Urakai-inhabited badlands to include appropriate communities of the other already-established peoples, including Ogres and whimsical or fairy-tale-feeling peoples. These are full intelligent peoples with family, political agency, economies, differing customs and serious as well as funny lives, not props, servants or uniformly comedic species. This complements the earlier requirement for multiple Eldar and Aelwyn elder communities, two human culture belts, Gnome/Pixie settlements, and Urakai cities in the southeastern wastes. No previously counted population is being added twice. Existing peoples to preserve across the wider atlas: Khazari, Eldar, Urakai, Humans, Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk, Pigfolk, Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk, Harpies; also rare/unquantified Drakari, Aelwyn Fae and Living Mountains. Do not conflate Aelwyn Fae with Pixies or Brownies; do not invent Mousefolk or import named fairy-tale characters without an explicit creator decision. No species is inherently good or evil because its look is fanciful. Proposed placement ecology and everyday life—not a fixed monopoly or new sovereign roster: - Giant expanded Letharion and western old-growth: Eldar courts, Ent grove federations, Aelwyn seasonal enclaves, Pixie canopy villages, Satyr/Faun orchards, Brownie/Boggart hedge/household boroughs, Mushroom-folk damp wood settlements, woodland Goblin and Gnome quarters, forest-friendly Troll households, and mixed hamlets with Halflings, Foxfolk and others. Protected and sparsely traveled sacred stretches remain between settled cores. - Western agrarian plains, river towns and temperate wetlands: Halfling farmers, Pigfolk bakers/millers, Cowfolk dairies, Foxfolk couriers/merchants, Gnome waterworks, Kobold brick/drainage guilds, Goblin markets, human river and estate cultures, Satyr orchards, river-loving Trolls and practical Ogre quarry/road/transport workers. Ogres may instead own businesses, hold offices, farm, study or simply live family lives; roles are options, not biological restrictions. - Far-west storm coast, western highlands, peninsulas and islands: Distinct human maritime culture, Wolvenkin and Bearfolk communities, Goblin and Gnome docks, Ogre and Giant upland settlements, Harpy cliff-side towns and courier routes, coastal Merfolk polities with negotiated shore access; perhaps Centaur grassland hinterlands and mixed Minotaur communities. Remote Drakari and Living Mountain possibilities remain unlocated and unquantified; their actual territories are not decided by illustrative dots. - Urakai southeastern badlands and wastes: Permanent Urakai canyon/well/volcanic-upland cities and tribal confederations, interspersed with Ogre families/clans and settlements, cave-and-quarry Goblins, Kobolds and Gnomes, Troll enclaves around springs/stone ravines, caravan-oriented Minotaurs and Centaurs along viable grazing fringes, small Harpy cliff settlements, and individual/mixed communities of Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Pigfolk, Foxfolk and humans wherever ecological and trade conditions allow. Arid regions require water, food, storage, routes, trade and craftsmanship. Do not imply all Ogres, Trolls or Goblins live in the wastes or are vassals of one Urakai monarch. Uninhabitable expanses remain genuinely empty. Map implementation: On a large private Khazari chart of Avarra show major established kingdoms and all seven correctly placed Throne cities around the Ironspine-encircled Veiled Inland Sea; leave a vast thousands-of-miles west; label enormous northern/western Letharion Forest, northwest coldlands, west rural plains and far-west port cultures, the southwestern Shattered Gulf, southern open country/Crown Sea and massive eastern/southeastern Urakai-populated wastes and badlands. Depict mixed-species villages, little forest boroughs, caravan cities and Ogre/Troll communities using subtle settlement glyphs or small illustrated vignettes without overwhelming broad geography. Inner-basin villages connect to each other by shore roads and ferries, but public outsiders lack ordinary passage. Do not invent or canonize new government names, exact census values, moon counts, dates or map scale bars from generated art; no character knowledge or campaign event changes. Demographic protection: Reuse the creator-adopted 6× modeled populations (Avarra 1,019.760m; world 2,062.800m), allocating already-existing continent and species totals into regionally plausible habitats rather than adding populations. Aelwyn and exceptional rare peoples still lack precise numeric censuses; existing birth rates and cultural diversity are unchanged. ## Era of Fire — third and final era of the Second Age, 116 years (creator canon, 21 November 2026) AVARRAN HISTORICAL NAME, CREATOR-ESTABLISHED: The third and final Avarran-defined era of Eryndor's Second Age is called the Era of Fire; other continents may name or divide the period differently. It lasted 116 years, corresponding to Second Age Years 1,322–1,437 inclusive. Its exact duration is derived from the already confirmed Second Age total: 1,437 − 321 years (Era of Awakening) − 1,000 years (Era of Wonder) = 116 years. Chronology: (1) Era of Awakening, Years 1–321, 321 years; (2) Era of Wonder, Years 322–1,321, 1,000 years; (3) Era of Fire, Years 1,322–1,437, 116 years. The catastrophic global earthquakes at the end of the Era of Fire ended the Second Age and began the Third Age. Their causes, seismic effects, sudden marshland and lowland mountain uplift, tenfold global aftershock amplification through the ancient Ironspine, mass deaths without whole-species extinction and the as-yet-undefined magical protection are recorded separately, not invented here. STRICTLY UNWRITTEN INTERIOR OF ERA: The creator explicitly requested no new racial, cultural, political, military, magical, religious or event history be filled into this third era yet. Only its name, length, place in the chronology and already creator-approved ending catastrophe are established. “Fire” has no confirmed source or metaphorical meaning; do not assume volcanoes, wars, dragons, burning moons, fire magic, apocalyptic conflagration, Fire Gods, or any particular ruler, kingdom, people or First Throne connection. The open First Throne storyline remains genuinely unselected; Gloin's ancestry and campaign scene remain unaffected. ## Urakai / Orcs — FIRST APPEAR IN THE THIRD AGE, absent from First and Second Ages (binding creator correction, 21 November 2026) CANON CHRONOLOGICAL RULE — supersedes conflicting earlier text: Urakai (Orcs) did not exist in the First Age or anywhere in the 1,437-year Second Age. The exiled dark mages of southeastern Avarra created the Orcs sometime during the Third Age. The exact Third Age year, creation method, first location, identities of the first communities, and subsequent structure of mage–Orc command remain UNDECIDED. The Orcs were absent from the Second Age's Era of Awakening (Years 1–321), Era of Wonder (Years 322–1,321) and Era of Fire (Years 1,322–1,437). Earlier lore depicting Orc inhabitants, clans, armies, cities or events in either of those two Ages is superseded and noncanon. Goblins and Ogres may predate the Third Age. CREATOR CANON — Third Age creation and intended conquests: The exiled dark mages who formed the southeastern Avarran Southern Wastes and its volcano during the Second Age survived well into the Third Age, when they created the Urakai (Orcs) by a method not yet decided. Their ambition in creating the Orcs was first to besiege the dwarven (Khazari) strongholds, and ultimately to attack the Eldar and human kingdoms. This establishes the mages' intentions, not any particular siege, conquest, campaign, chronology, victory or attack as an accomplished fact. The mages established no diplomacy, trade, treaties or alliances with pre-existing outside peoples; creating the Orcs is an act of creation for the mages' ambitions, not evidence of diplomatic relations. The exact magical or other creation process, timing, first Orc settlements, degree and duration of mage control, and later independence or resistance remain open. The modern Urakai are a diverse people with their own cultures and agency; they are not collectively evil, personally culpable for the mages' acts, or necessarily still subject to their creators. Effects on war histories: Any established older east–west wars involving Urakai, and any historical Goblin/Ogre alliances or assistance with Orc forces, must have happened in the Third Age or later, with no specific Age within that range, reign, battle, migration date or formal state assigned yet. The anti-Goblin, anti-Ogre and anti-Urakai prejudices of western Avarra remain valid consequences of those undated wars. These cannot predate the Third Age. Nor should living Urakai's settled southeast badlands homelands and their modern peoples/cultures be erased or treated as magically evil due to a speculative ancient link. Canon controls and campaign: Modern Urakai exist in large numbers, with sophisticated diverse societies, independent cities, families, economies, politics, culture and varied morality. Existing Fifth Age maps and sixfold census are unchanged; this corrects only their ancestral chronology. No changes to family rates, species lifespans or present demographics. The no-species-extinction rule at the Second Age-ending earthquake stays: Urakai were not a species that survived that disaster, because they had not appeared yet; all peoples existing at that time survived somewhere. Do not connect their origin to Gloin Hammerfeld's genuinely unknown genealogy, the First Throne, the lost First Age moon-magics or the yet-unexplained global species-survival magical force without an explicit new creator decision. ## Second Age racial histories III — eight sentient animal-featured peoples (Awakening and Wonder ONLY, creator-authorized expansion, 21 November 2026) Chronology: These histories belong to the Era of Awakening (Second Age Years 1–321) and Era of Wonder (Years 322–1,321) alone. They are culturally diverse ancestral strands, not automatic biographies of all descendants or the founding dates of present-day states. Biology, magical talent and moral worth never follow from animal resemblance alone. ### Wolvenkin — loyalty tested by necessity - Awakening: Neighbors formed rescue watches across forests, mountains and river settlements when protective magic failed. Some Wolvenkin households made a point of helping strangers beyond their own kin, while others kept stores within the family. Cooperative tracking and physically marked safe paths became respected skills in many communities. - Wonder: New lunar arts helped certain scouts and healers with distant signaling, restorative care and safe travel. Wolvenkin groups also became prominent in mixed neighborhood councils and long-distance trade. Their social structures remained diverse; no universal pack hierarchy, compulsory leadership style or shared homeland is added. ### Foxfolk — the difference between a bargain and a miracle - Awakening: Foxfolk merchants, farmers and urban families developed careful ways to verify magical guarantees when charms could fail or change. A witnessed contract, a stored tool and a truthful account of losses mattered more than a clever-sounding promise. Some fooled the unwary, while others became sought-after honest mediators. - Wonder: Schools of enchantment appraisal, illusionary performance, navigation and commercial arbitration flourished among various Foxfolk populations. Such skills could enrich a thriving city or be abused by a dishonest guild. Their diverse livelihoods contradict the later stereotype that a clever face means deception. ### Lionfolk — honor in rebuilding - Awakening: Communities in warm plains, savannas and cities disputed who bore responsibility for vulnerable neighbors when magical protections broke. Some developed public rescue duties and direct dispute hearings; others centered family property and guarded resources. Courage was a valued act, not a biological guarantee. - Wonder: Oratory, civic law, scholarship, healing and new protective magical disciplines became subjects of pride in different Lionfolk circles. Rival traditions favored magnanimous service, competitive excellence or private accomplishment. No single Lionfolk dynasty or universal savanna monarchy is dated to this era. ### Tigerfolk — careful craft under changing skies - Awakening: Jungle, river and city communities studied dangerous changes in moon-influenced weather, forest paths and protective workings. Field observers compared ordinary tracks, plant life and water levels with unreliable divination instead of trusting spells alone. Many chose art, family or commerce rather than the stereotyped hunter's life. - Wonder: Specialist schools explored new moon magic in medicine, architecture, craft precision and woodland navigation. Some communities favored quiet scientific practice, others public magical arts and civic scholarship. Skill was learned, not universally inherited by species. ### Elephantfolk — water and remembered obligations - Awakening: Families and local councils took special care to document canal depths, flood marks, water allotments and ordinary construction techniques after enchanted water control became unpredictable. Long community memory could help, but no First Age written testimony survived, and no Elephantfolk retained infallible knowledge of the lost world. - Wonder: Large-scale irrigation expertise, teaching traditions, medicine and new environmental magic supported prosperous mixed settlements. Different Elephantfolk circles quarreled over whether public water should be a shared right or owned by powerful patrons. Their abilities and political beliefs varied by individual and locality. ### Bearfolk — the shelter that still holds - Awakening: Coldland and temperate communities restored plain heating, dry storage and storm shelters where moon-touched household protections failed. Networks of hospitable waystations existed alongside isolationist families and ruthless toll collectors. Strength did not imply kindness or leadership. - Wonder: Newly mastered lunar practices enriched winter medicine, protective architecture, crafted comforts and long-distance trade. Some Bearfolk excelled as judges, makers or travelers, while others rejected public life. They did not all live in northern forests or share identical hibernation biology. ### Cowfolk — prosperity rooted in ordinary land - Awakening: Mixed grazing, farming and market settlements learned to keep reliable water, soil knowledge and feed supplies despite failures in plant growth enchantments. Some Cowfolk communities became respected for cooperative food reserves, but urban residents, soldiers and scholars also took part. - Wonder: New lunar agricultural arts were integrated with soil rotation, garden medicine, market networks and city infrastructure. Prosperity could support large households and cosmopolitan guilds, while disputes over land ownership and exploitation remained. No compulsory farmer identity or uniform family structure is created. ### Pigfolk — practical invention and the feast of work - Awakening: Pigfolk households and urban workers managed sanitation, cooking fuels, food storage, repair trades and community distribution as magic failed unevenly. Some celebrated collective kitchens, others guarded private workshops or sought advantage amid scarcity. - Wonder: Newly stable lunar arts encouraged fine craft, creative food culture, medicine, industrial experimentation and celebrated public markets. A Pigfolk master machinist, philosopher, entrepreneur or quiet parent was as plausible as a farmer. Regional cultures differed and prosperity brought familiar labor and property disputes. Shared magical history: The First Age's extinct moon-specific magics remain truly gone; the Era of Wonder involved mastery of newer moon-fragment powers without replacing independent planetary Natural Magic. No specific present-day society or named city is automatically transplanted more than a millennium into the past. This earlier chapter concentrated on the first two Avarran eras; the third Avarran era is now covered in the dedicated Era of Fire chronicle and broader Second Age Annals. ## How animal-featured cultures differ from simple animal stereotypes - Their households, cities, clans, courts, occupations and trade networks reflect real social histories and material life, not animal fables taken literally. - A Foxfolk family need not be deceitful; a Wolvenkin lawyer may mistrust the group around her; a shy Lionfolk farmer may dislike giving speeches; a Pigfolk warrior may be austere. The right to contradict reputation is fundamental. - Families can be large, intergenerational, adoptive, childless, single-parent, communal or spread across settlements as allowed by established species biology. Do not insert new “litters,” mating instincts or breeding rates simply because an animal resembles the species. - Regional subcultures may take cultural traits from neighbors, especially in Bramblebridge and other mixed communities. That adaptation does not make the people identical to their human, Goblin or Khazari neighbors. - A frightening individual can cause real harm; a respected citizen can betray a city. Wrongdoing is personal and institutional, not racial fate. ## Wolvenkin — competing meanings of loyalty | Distinct subculture | Location and what earns esteem | Family and conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | Wintermark Watch Hearths | Northern Avarra garrison towns: disciplined guarding, public rescue, careful observation | Kin care and regiment bonds overlap; some officers mistake obedience for integrity | | Tharvorn Snow-Track Families | Boreal forests: winter guides, reindeer care, careful use of food, keeping promises | Isolation breeds proud independence; guests face difficult etiquette | | Stonewake Border Wardens | Karak-Varn approaches: mountain tracking, joint Khazari–Wolvenkin patrol craft | Mixed court law, competition for guard contracts and suspicion from outsiders | | Orundel Reed Scouts | Rivers and wetlands: local knowledge, public warning, education, family fisheries | Others undervalue tracking as intellectual skill; scouts dispute hunting rights | | Free Lantern Townfolk | Bramblebridge and market cities: bakeries, carpentry, politics, theater, scholarship | Some resent being recruited into guard work on appearance alone | Wolvenkin personal freedom: Devotion to kin, colleague or chosen companions can be admired, but a lone wanderer may be genuinely respected. An individual who betrays a particular promise is judged for that action; being Wolvenkin is not an automatic promise of loyalty. ## Foxfolk — wit can serve courts, farms or fraud | Distinct subculture | Place and what it celebrates | Family and dilemmas | | --- | --- | --- | | Shattered Coast Tide-Quills | Republic ports: negotiation, law, colorful theatre, navigation and market arbitration | Guild alliances can be exploitative; honesty can outshine clever deceit | | Vaelora Foxglade Households | Lake-and-orchard towns: household stewardship, gardening, hospitality, poetry | Rural elders dislike courtly polish and city youths resist marriage pressure | | Tharvorn Frost-Tale Lodges | Northern woods: hunting knowledge, stories, winter trade and hospitality | Rival storykeepers contest ownership of ancient tales | | Orundel Marsh-Court Traders | River wetlands: waterborne messages, bridge toll law, medicinal marsh plants | Sharp negotiators may be resented by neighbors dependent on their service | | Bramblebridge Hearth Factors | Western Avarra mixed village: recordkeeping, crafts, friendly commercial humor | Outsiders' trickster stereotypes can lead to unjust suspicion | Family: Family-run shops, extended kin, solo itinerant traders and chosen mentor households are valid. Some value shrewdness, others public honesty or generosity. Fraud is not an inherited trait. ## Lionfolk — different ideals of dignity and courage | Subculture | Region and respected paths | Local conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | Jade Savannah Councillors | Sahrad pastoral cities: mediation, fair protection, public responsibility and calm courage | Elder houses may monopolize council positions | | Sahradi River-Guard Families | Oasis and river towns: caravan safety, justice, water protection | Militant leaders sometimes mistake dominance for protection | | Orundel Crownstep Scholars | River and savanna academies: legal argument, ethics, histories and diplomacy | Traditional warriors may mock quiet achievement | | Avarran Honor-Merchants | Cosmopolitan cities: transparent contracts, gift customs, protecting dependents | Reputation disputes and duels can be destructive | | Vaelora Wandering Healers | Sparse diaspora: disciplined medicine, patient instruction, service | Rare visitors face public curiosity and suspicion | Family: Large intergenerational councils and informal village households can both exist; do not infer mandatory biological prides. A humble Lionfolk cook or shy playwright can be fully respectable. ## Tigerfolk — precision is only one possible virtue | Subculture | Place and esteemed work | Frictions | | --- | --- | --- | | Orundel Rainpath Clans | Jungle river villages: patient planning, environmental observation, herbal care | Land development threatens village independence | | Mangrove Crown Trade Houses | Large eastern cities: shipping, sophisticated debate, public education | Commercial elites versus poorer waterfront laborers | | Sahrad Greenbelt Families | Humid southern coast: fishing, farming, rescue and practical innovation | River water control disputes with neighboring estates | | Vaelora Lakegarden Artisans | Diaspora in lake towns: textiles, music, medicine, private scholarship | Distant kin sometimes regard assimilation as lost identity | | Western Road Soloists | Avarra travel routes: wandering craftsmen, explorers, mercenary specialists | Their choice of solitude is not species biology nor compulsory exile | Family: A Tigerfolk hunter can raise a busy household; an urban lecturer may have no desire to fight; an aloof family elder may nonetheless cherish descendants. “Always solitary” is inaccurate. ## Elephantfolk — historical memory and civic engineering take varied forms | Subculture | Region and celebrated roles | Disagreement | | --- | --- | --- | | Jade Savannah Memory Courts | Sahrad: ancestral oral history, water management, intergenerational teaching | Some traditions overprivilege noble ancestry | | Oliford Barge Families | Sahradi river towns: heavy water transport, flood works, cooperative supply | Ferry monopolies versus common access | | Orundel Riverwright Councils | Great river cities: hydraulic design, record archives, law, public works | Engineers and spiritual custodians dispute canal changes | | Crane Hollow Gardeners | Orundel village: community care, orchards and fine-scale craft | Oversimplified outsider assumptions that their strength determines job | | Western Diaspora Tutors | Vaelora/Avarra ports: foreign-language teaching and shared archives | Minority communities fight exploitative employment contracts | Family: It is possible to have close cousins across decades and full multigenerational gatherings, but a person's memory is not automatically infallible and history may be contested. No invented breeding interval or mandatory herd structure. ## Bearfolk — comfort, resilience and leadership need not coincide | Subculture | Region and respectable roles | Source of conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | Bearcross Hearthmasters | Northern Holds: hospitality, winter care, robust construction, hunting safety | Aristocratic lodges seek to monopolize forests | | Tharvorn Greyberry Collectives | Cold woodlands: stored provisions, family fishing and seasonal mutual help | Hoarding accusations can divide neighbors | | Vaelora Lakewood Stewards | Great lakes: forestry, fisheries, artisan timber trade and kin networks | Commercial logging versus sacred woodland claims | | Orundel Highwood Travelers | Small mountain enclaves: guiding, intercity exchange, mountain medicine | Rare visitors are treated as dangerous outsiders | | Urban Tea-House Bearfolk | Avarra capitals and ports: cooks, innkeepers, scholars, civic politicians | Stereotypes that Bearfolk are either lazy or violent | Families and humor: Extended family feasts and solitary contemplative life are not mutually exclusive. An elderly Bearfolk judge may be brisk and demanding; a young Bearfolk musician can be shy. Social respect may hinge on hospitality in one valley and daring travel in another. ## Cowfolk — farming is an option, not a destiny | Subculture | Location and admired paths | Tensions | | --- | --- | --- | | Longpasture Commons | Aldermere farms: land stewardship, animal care, dairies and negotiated common rights | Noble enclosures and bad herd disease | | Orundel Riverwheel Guilds | Agricultural cities: trade, school maintenance, grain storage and technical craft | Rich merchant families against cooperative millers | | Sunthatch Hearth Families | Eastern Avarran mixed farming towns: kin protection, village law, practical agriculture | Border conflict and pasture disputes | | Sahradi Irrigation Households | Nile-like river valleys: canal monitoring, merchants, skilled artisans | Water pressure and legal status conflicts | | Vaelora Lake Traders | Western markets: farming, boat crews, politics, fine arts | Outsiders expect every Cowfolk to be patient and passive | Family: Cooperative homes and extended relatives are prominent in many districts, but single adults and urban professional life are entirely valid. Gentle temperament cannot be assumed; household disputes and militant resistance can occur. ## Pigfolk — food culture, ambition and craft are diverse | Subculture | Region and admired paths | Disagreement | | --- | --- | --- | | Bramblebridge Mill Families | Western Avarra mixed-species market town: baking, civic service, mill maintenance and cheerful competition | Flour monopoly, council taxes, village class politics | | Vaelora Lakeharbor Dock Houses | Lakes and ports: shipping, cooperative accounts, freight labor and tavern culture | Dockworkers versus powerful cargo financiers | | Orundel Riverwheel Growers | River villages: wetland farms, mill machinery, family education | Floodplain land rights and merchant monopolies | | Sahradi Reedvoice Households | Wetlands: fungi partnership, textile reeds, boat work and medicine | Drought and unequal canal allocations | | Avarran Roadhouse Cooks | Traveling inns, camps and fairs: hospitality, cooking, trade craft and safe rest | Roving families challenged by settled landlords | No animal-fable default: Neither “always hungry” nor “always greedy” defines Pigfolk, and they are not inevitable victims of predatory species. A Pigfolk tax collector, general, artisan, philosopher, protest organizer or physician is normal within the range of possible individuals. ## Mixed animal-featured communities and distinctive local identities In some cities, animal-featured peoples share a neighborhood identity stronger than species affiliation. Examples: | Local community | Its composite culture | Tensions that make it real | | --- | --- | --- | | Bramblebridge Free Hearth Wards | Pigfolk, Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Halflings, Goblins, Brownies, Gnomes and others share bridge festivals, market courts and family invitations | A new safety ordinance may disproportionately affect tiny or very large residents | | Tanglelock Ferry District | Foxfolk, Tigerfolk, Pigfolk, Kobolds, Minotaurs, humans and others cooperate on wetland transport | Competing toll systems, flood protection, class and labor disputes | | Candleburrow Winter Hall | Bearfolk, Wolvenkin, Goblins, Trolls, Ogres, Brownies and humans have shared firewood and winter-food rules | Wealthy woodlot owners fight a shelter policy | | Jade Savannah Canal Commons | Lionfolk, Elephantfolk, Minotaurs, Centaurs, humans and others take part in water courts | Herds, field agriculture and irrigation compete | | Lakeharbor Free Boat Quarters | Pigfolk, Cowfolk, Foxfolk, Gnomes, humans and Merfolk visiting freshwater exchange basins | Boats, docks, legal boundaries and housing costs | Mixed-town consequences: A Wolvenkin judge and Pigfolk merchant can share civic identity, but may speak different household languages. Inter-species adoptive kin is possible socially where lawful; offspring between unrelated species is not established biologically. Some communities are warm, others discriminatory; injustice can be perpetrated by any people against their own or others. A dramatic attack, kidnapping, political arrest or slave raid is possible but not pre-scripted. ## Professions and social choices — protected rules - No profession is biologically assigned to animal-featured peoples. Strength, senses and body shape affect what is physically convenient but do not define education, ambition, compassion, class or morality. - Some households combine fame and family; some ordinary workers raise large families; some scholars and crafters remain unmarried; some individuals switch life paths repeatedly. The creator's no birth-rate changes instruction applies to every group. - A social ideal is not an objective law of Eryndor: a celebrated leader may be cruel, a marginalized person competent, and a local council mistaken. - Regional culture is the combination of where the person grew up, who raised them, which institutions influenced them and their choices—not just a species label. ## Connections Eryndor Living Culture Atlas VIII — Thrones, Eldar, Urakai, Humans & Elder Courts · Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — Smaller Peoples & Regional Traditions · Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads.
